intro: In a busy New York churchyard, an old gravestone carries a line of tiny shapes. In a green and gold book from the 1700s, page after page is filled with symbols nobody could read. Both hold real messages. Both were made by members of secret societies who wanted to share words with each other, and keep them from everyone else.

In this unit, you will become a codebreaker. You will learn the pigpen cipher and read the message on James Leeson's stone. You will count letters the way codebreakers have for more than a thousand years. You will follow three researchers who used computers and language skills to crack the Copiale Cipher in 2011.

You will also meet stonemasons in Scotland who were tested on their memory in 1599. By the end, you will be able to make and break a simple cipher, explain how a key works, and build a memory palace of your own. You will also practice asking: what does the evidence really show?
bigQuestion: Why did secret societies hide their words in codes, and how do people unlock them?

timeline.t: Julius Caesar sends private letters in a shift cipher, a Roman writer later reports.
In Baghdad, al-Kindi writes the oldest known guide to breaking ciphers by counting letters.
Agrippa's book shows letters hidden in a grid, an early ancestor of pigpen.
William Schaw writes his first rules for Scottish stonemasons' lodges.
Schaw's second rules tell the Kilwinning lodge to test masons on the art of memory.
Freemasons use the pigpen cipher widely, and it becomes known as the Masonic cipher.
Someone writes the Copiale Cipher, a 105-page book of symbols and letters.
James Leeson dies; his New York gravestone carries a pigpen line.
A Masonic ceremony book is written in cipher as a private study aid.
Kevin Knight, Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer crack the Copiale Cipher.

words.d: a way of hiding a message by changing each letter into another letter or symbol
a system that swaps whole words or ideas for other words or signs
a secret alphabet where each letter is written as the shape of its space on a grid or an X
the message in plain words before it is hidden
the message after it has been hidden with a cipher
the rule, number or chart used to hide a message and to read it again
a cipher that swaps each letter for another letter or symbol, always by the same rule
breaking a cipher by counting how often each letter or symbol appears
Latin words meaning "remember that you will die"; a reminder to live well
a cipher that gives common letters several different symbols, so counting is harder
a secret society of the 1700s whose ceremonies were built around eyes and seeing
a way to remember things by picturing them in spots along a place you know well

test.q: In the pigpen cipher, what stands for each letter?
choices: The shape of the letter's space on a grid or X
test.why: Pigpen writes each letter as the shape of its pen on the key.

test.q: Why is pigpen often called the Masonic cipher?
choices: Freemasons used it widely from the 1700s
It was found in the Copiale
test.why: The grid idea is older, but Freemasons took it up and spread it, so it got their name.

test.q: What does the pigpen line on James Leeson's gravestone say?
test.why: Decoded with the key, the Leeson stone reads REMEMBER DEATH.

test.q: What is the difference between a code and a cipher?
choices: A code uses shapes and a cipher uses numbers
A code swaps whole words, and a cipher swaps letters
A cipher is always harder to break
A code can only be spoken
test.why: A code replaces whole words or ideas. A cipher changes single letters.

test.q: In a shift cipher with a shift of three, what does B become?
test.why: Moving B three places along the alphabet gives E.

test.q: Why must the key to a cipher be kept safe?
choices: Because the key is part of the plaintext
Because keys can only be used once
Because anyone with the key can read the message
test.why: A cipher is only as strong as the secret of its key.

test.q: Which letter is the most common in English?
test.why: E appears about 12.7 times in every 100 letters, more than any other letter.

choices: Hiding a key inside a book
Counting how often letters or symbols appear to break a cipher
Remembering things with a memory palace
test.why: Frequency analysis uses letter counts to guess what each symbol stands for.

test.q: Which statement about the Copiale Cipher is correct?
choices: It is a gravestone in Scotland
It was written by Julius Caesar
It is a 105-page book from about 1730, cracked in 2011
test.why: The Copiale is a 105-page book dated to about 1730. It was cracked in 2011.

test.q: Why did the Copiale's homophonic cipher make counting harder?
choices: Common letters were split among several symbols
It used no letters at all
test.why: When E has several symbols, no single symbol stands out as the most common.

test.q: How did computers and people share the work on the Copiale?
choices: Computers counted and matched patterns; people tested guesses and read the German
Computers did all the work alone
People did all the counting by hand
Computers read the German and people typed it
test.why: The computer counted and compared patterns, but people had to test guesses and make sense of the words.

test.q: Which word led the team to the Oculists?
test.why: Megyesi noticed a symbol for eye, and Schaefer linked the book to the Oculists.

test.q: Compare the Leeson stone and the Copiale. What do both show?
choices: Both were written by Julius Caesar
Both used a cipher to share words with members of a group
test.why: The Leeson stone used a Masonic cipher, and the Copiale hid a society's ceremonies. Both shared words with members.

test.q: What did the 1599 Schaw Statutes ask masons at Kilwinning to be tested on?
test.why: Schaw's second rules told the lodge to test every mason and apprentice on the art of memory.

choices: A real palace where Masons met
A way to remember by picturing things in spots along a place you know
test.why: A memory palace places things to remember in spots along a familiar place, then you walk through it in your mind.

write.prompt: Why did secret societies hide their words in codes? Use the Leeson stone, the Copiale Cipher and the Schaw Statutes. Cite at least two facts from the unit, and explain how members and critics might see the same secret differently.
tips: Name each source you use, such as the Leeson gravestone (1794) or the Copiale Cipher (about 1730).
Give one reason members kept secrets and one worry critics had.
Use unit words like cipher, key and frequency analysis.
Say what the evidence shows, and what it does not show.
Plan with a memory palace or a short list before you write.
